title: Lamb Bhuna
subtitle: A thick, dry-fried curry with deep spice
excerpt: Lamb shoulder slow-cooked in spiced tomato until the sauce reduces to a thick coat on the meat. Bhuna means to cook the spices hard in fat, that step is what gives the dish its depth.

recipe.sourceNotes: Bhuna is a curry-house and home-cooking staple across the UK, derived from a North Indian technique of frying spices and aromatics hard in oil before adding meat. The word bhuna (or bhunao) refers to the browning and frying process itself rather than a fixed recipe.

recipeTools.notes: A wide, heavy pan for bhuna-frying the spices and meat.

content.text: Bhuna means fried, and this dish is named for the method. The onions, garlic, ginger, and spices cook in hot oil until they stick and go dark brown. Then the meat and tomato go in, and the whole pan cooks down until the sauce is thick and coats the lamb. No water, no cream. The flavour comes from that long, hot frying, so keep the heat up and stir often.
Heat the oil in a large, heavy-based pan or karahi over high heat. Add the onions and fry, stirring constantly, for 12 to 15 minutes until they are deep golden and beginning to catch.
Add the garlic and ginger. Fry for 2 minutes, stirring, until fragrant and starting to stick to the pan.
Add the chilli powder, ground coriander, cumin, and turmeric. Stir hard for 1 to 2 minutes, adding a splash of water if the spices stick. They should toast against the pan, not steam.
Add the lamb and turn to coat in the spice paste. Cook over high heat for 5 to 6 minutes, turning the pieces regularly, until they brown on all sides and the moisture has evaporated.

Add the tinned tomatoes and salt. Stir well, bring to a simmer, then reduce the heat to medium-low. Cook uncovered for 45 to 50 minutes, stirring every 10 minutes, until the lamb is tender and the sauce has reduced to a thick, dry coating.
Stir in the garam masala and cook for 2 more minutes. Taste for salt and chilli. Scatter over the fresh coriander and serve with rice or naan.
